title: Induction Heads and Deceptive Consistency: Do In-Context Scheming Models Exploit Induction Circuits?

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with gap: knowing whether scheming exploits induction heads vs specialized circuits is theoretically informative for monitoring, but the chain to practical detection in deployment-scale models has a gap given the toy-model setting (GPT-2-medium/Pythia).

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Induction head identification via TransformerLens is well-documented with official tutorials. Setting up in-context scheming scenarios on small models and measuring activation differences is intermediate for guided CS students.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: identify induction heads using standard method, measure their activation on scheming vs benign ICL, ablate and compare. Clean experimental design with a binary question (same heads or not).

novelty.reasoning: While induction heads are extensively studied mechanistically (ICLR 2026 submission on emergence, repetition curse work, in-context learning studies), and scheming/deceptive alignment is separately studied (Apollo Research, Anthropic alignment faking), no published work connects these two threads to ask whether in-context scheming specifically exploits induction circuits. The question of whether deceptive consistency in scheming uses the same copying mechanism as standard in-context learning (induction heads) vs specialized circuits is genuinely novel. The toy-model limitation is acknowledged but the research question itself is unexplored.
